newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. Holocaust writer admits flaws, angers Germans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Holocaust writer admits flaws, angers Germans.

text.p: An outspoken American Holocaust scholar whose book "Hitler's Willing Executioners" has upset Germans has launched a speaking tour in this country by unexpectedly agreeing his hard-hitting work had flaws.

Harvard University sociologist Daniel Goldhagen, at his first public appearance in Germany since his book appeared, insisted on Wednesday evening his angry work was still the best attempt yet to explain how a civilised nation like Germany could have slaughtered six million Jews during World War Two.

But he surprised the audience in a packed Hamburg theatre for his debate with five German historians and journalists by conceding he had underestimated how other factors mixed with a virulent anti-Semitism to lead to the Third Reich's crimes.

The best-selling book, which passionately argues almost all pre-war Germans were obsessed by a burning desire to kill Jews, has sparked a heated debate here that shows how the Holocaust still haunts Germany half a century later.
The fact this sweeping indictment of the Germans comes from an American Jew who is the son of a Romanian Holocaust survivor has added further tension to the testy discussion here.

"I skirted over some of this history a little too quickly," Goldhagen told Reuters Television on Thursday while discussing critics' charges his stark portrayal of German anti-Semitism before Hitler came to power in 1933 was too simply drawn.

"Now that I've had some time to reflect upon the book, I think one thing I would devote more attention to and integrate into the analysis is the effect of the First World War in radicalising German society."

Mainstream German historians say a tragic mix of factors including the trauma of losing World War One, the economic depression and fear of a communist revolution joined with anti-Semitism to lead Germans and Jews to disaster. Analyses based mostly on a single explanation miss the point, they say.

Several of the 400 Germans in the audience said they were disappointed that Goldhagen, who has vehemently defended his book and blasted his German critics in print, simply agreed with some key objections when discussing them in person.

"That bothered me," Sy Esterer, a public relations executive, said after the two-hour debate. "I was astonished to see how he conceded so many points and then changed the subject," high school student Bele Freudenberg commented.

The panelists, who sat at black-draped tables in a stage setting as sombre as a wake, agreed Goldhagen was right to say historians should shift their focus from the Nazis themselves to what went on in the minds of the rank-and-file killers.

While praising other parts of his book, they avoided debating his core theory about the uniqueness of German anti-Semitism so politely that the moderator had to urge them to get around to the real flash point of the debate.

Hannes Heer, a Hamburg historian who has documented the Wehrmacht's role in slaughtering Jews on the Eastern Front, even publicly apologised for a scathing review of Goldhagen's book he had published in a Berlin newspaper that morning.
"I didn't mean to hurt his feelings," he said.
Goldhagen, who plans more public debates in Berlin and Munich during his one-week tour, said he had no idea why his 461-page book was more critically received in Germany than in the United States.
He denied it was a blanket condemnation of the Germans, as critics in this country have charged, and said many Germans agreed with him after reading his book.
Some critics had not even read the book before tearing it apart, he said, and well-known historians had spread lies about it to discredit it and discourage Germans from buying it.
"That's the real story of this book," he said.
